It applies 3A.4: the modifier is known at the start of Fire, Update and Restore until the first change to the collection, and during Create only through the field's value. It refuses both examples, leaves item 12's modifier question open, and says the other documents mean this. Added a draft-marked paragraph after proof-engine.md's Modifier-proof strategy. It says the built strategy discharges at every site, which is an unsound implementation gap, and points to the spec. The collection-types repair is described above.

findings.title: runtime-api.md cites a heading that no longer exists and says every global rule is true of the current version
findings.reason: runtime-api.md:346 cites '*Between operations nothing is carried except the rules*', which is no longer a heading. It also restates the rule as 'global rules and in ensures whose guards hold', leaving out the spec's exclusions for rules that mention now() or a field the state omits.
findings.repair: Replaced the restatement at runtime-api.md (Applicable constraints bullet) with a pointer to the current heading, 'Between operations nothing is carried except what every reachable configuration satisfies'. It names the two exclusions as examples and does not restate the rule.

findings.title: runtime-api.md cites a heading that does not exist, and claims more is known between operations than 3A.4 allows
findings.reason: Same defect as the previous finding, plus the Tier 2 Scope Rules paragraph, which restates the same overbroad claim. If the claim were read as covering rules that mention now(), it would assume an answer to the outstanding owner decision.
findings.repair: Also rewrote the Tier 2 Scope Rules sentence in runtime-api.md so that it defers to the spec heading. Neither runtime-api passage now says anything about now() rules beyond pointing to the spec, which assumes no answer.

findings.title: result-types.md says a preview's ArgErrors is structural only and stops constraint evaluation; the spec and evaluator.md say it covers every phase-1 failure and is collect-all
findings.reason: Spec §3A.6 rule 2 and §3A.4 phase 1 make preview ingress the whole of phase 1: argument constraints and event ensures included, collect-all. evaluator.md:1046 agrees. result-types.md:205, :214 and :279 described a structural-only check that stops all constraint evaluation. Under that reading, an ensure-only failure would leave OverallProspect unforced while Fire returns InvalidArgs.
findings.repair: In docs/runtime/result-types.md, rewrote the ArgErrors field comment and bullet to cover the whole phase-1 check, collect-all, and to point to spec §3A.4 phase 1 and §3A.6 rule 2. When the list is non-empty, nothing after phase 1 is evaluated and the prospect is Impossible. Rewrote the ArgError description the same way, and noted that a failure belonging to no single argument does not fit ArgName. That shape question is now joined to the existing open note on the shape InvalidArgs needs, not decided. Fixed the matching field comment in docs/runtime/evaluator.md.

findings.title: The description of UpdateInspection names a member the record does not have, and assumes a patch can be incomplete
findings.reason: The UpdateInspection record declares only Fields, Constraints and Events, yet the bullets described a HypotheticalResult member gated on 'the patch is complete'. Spec §3A.6 says every patch, the empty one included, is a complete input. This was already listed as a mechanical drift item and had not been repaired.
findings.repair: Removed the HypotheticalResult bullet from result-types.md. Added two sentences after 'Returned by Version.InspectUpdate': a patch that fails ingress is not applied and nothing is recomputed from it (spec §3A.6 rule 2), and every patch is a complete input (spec §3A.6, When inputs are missing). A stale `RowInspection.HypotheticalResult` row in evaluator.md's guarantees table (around line 1953) names an older type and was left untouched as out of this finding's scope.

findings.title: A preview can evaluate a row after one whose guard is certainly true, when an earlier guard is undetermined
findings.reason: Spec 3A.6 stopped evaluation only once a row had 'certainly won dispatch', and result-types.md made later rows Impossible only after a Certain row. With an earlier undetermined guard, a later row whose guard is certainly true is only Possible, so the text allowed evaluating rows the operation can never reach. That breaks 3A.6 rule 2. The evaluator pseudocode (winnerFound on any certainly true guard) was already right.
findings.repair: Spec 3A.6 rule 2: once a row's guard is certainly true, no later row is evaluated, whether or not that row has certainly won; the report wording now says 'an earlier row's guard is certainly true'. result-types.md prospect propagation rules and the Prospect and PostFields descriptions were changed to match.

findings.title: A wrongly typed patch value is ConstraintsFailed in the spec but InvalidFields in result-types
findings.reason: Spec 3A.2 item 4 put a wrong-type patch value under ConstraintsFailed. result-types.md, evaluator.md (:362, :1857) and runtime-api.md all give a type mismatch as InvalidFields, and ConstraintsFailed as constraint violations only.
findings.repair: Spec 3A.2 item 4 now lists only constraint violations for a patch (ConstraintsFailed, pointing to result-types.md § UpdateOutcome). Item 9 now states that an undeclared field name or a value of the wrong type is InvalidFields, and that how one refused patch reports several kinds of failure is open in result-types.

findings.title: Evaluator ingress pseudocode skips a guarded event ensure whole when its body reads a bad argument
findings.reason: Spec phase 1, 'A guarded event ensure', makes the guard and the body two separate evaluations, with a false guard passing the ensure. evaluator.md ValidateIngress checked the guard's and body's arguments together, so the ensure was never added to `passed`, and ensures proved from it went unevaluated. That changes what collect-all reports.
findings.repair: evaluator.md ValidateIngress: a guarded ensure first evaluates its guard (needing only the guard's arguments and premises). A false guard adds the ensure to `passed` without evaluating the body; a true guard leads to the body being evaluated under its own arguments and premises. ValidateIngressForPreview is described as the same check, so it inherits the fix.

findings.title: Restore writes persisted values at phase 0, before phase 1 checks that they are declared and well typed
findings.reason: Phase 0 injected the persisted state and values, and decided which fields were omitted, before phase 1's structural check. That needs writes that cannot be made for an undeclared state or field, or for a mistyped value.
findings.repair: Phase 0 now has Restore make the structural check first and write nothing if it fails; only then does slot injection run. This is a design decision, so it carries reasoning, alternatives rejected, precedent and the tradeoff accepted. Phase 1 now points to phase 0 for the check, and the phase table rows for Restore were updated.

findings.title: The between-operations rule ends in a truncated sentence
findings.reason: The sentence at spec :2405 ended with 'with the one exception that entry states (...)', so it did not say which fields the exception covers.
findings.repair: The exception is now written out: a field the initial state omits, in a configuration in the initial state, where a construction row writes that field. It points to the second entry of 'What is known', which gives the reason.

findings.title: D132 read by purpose for a capture but by wording for an entry action
findings.reason: The outcome follows canon: D132 places the assignment in 'the transition action chain' and calls itself the dual of InitialEventMissingAssignments, which names the construction row. But the reason the draft gave for excluding entry actions ('may be guarded') does not cover an unguarded one. The capture rule and the entry-action rule also answer different questions (which kinds of write count, and where the write must be), and the draft never said so. Changing the outcome would go past D132's stated placement, so the repair is to the reasons only.
findings.repair: Spec 3A.4 Configurations (omitted field): the exclusion now rests on D132's placement ('guarded or not') and states that the capture rule decides which kinds of write count, not where the write must be. It carries reasoning, alternatives rejected, precedent and the tradeoff accepted (a redundant write in the row where an unguarded entry action always assigns the field). The phase 0 construction text now points to that reason instead of the 'two reasons'. The capture paragraph now says a capture meets D132 or InitialEventMissingAssignments only where it is in the row's own action chain.

findings.title: compiler-and-runtime-design.md defines Rejected as 'a row matched'
findings.reason: Lines 851 and 860 restated the outcome meanings and contradicted spec 3A.2 and phase 2, where Create returns Rejected when no construction guard is true. They also contradicted the document's own commit-outcome table.
findings.repair: Both definitions were rewritten. Unmatched and Rejected for Fire are now stated with Create's no-guard-true case as Rejected, and both point to spec § 3A.2.

findings.title: Per-operation matrix says InspectUpdate does no row dispatch and checks only the patch
findings.reason: Spec 3A.6 has InspectUpdate preview each event with rows in the current state, which includes that event's ingress and its row dispatch, when the patch would be accepted.
findings.repair: The InspectUpdate row of the matrix in compiler-and-runtime-design.md now adds, after the patch, the event previews run with no arguments, and row dispatch 'yes for each event it then previews'. It points to spec § 3A.6.

findings.title: collection-types.md says a failed append-by uniqueness guard ends Unmatched, which is wrong for construction
findings.reason: The sentence restated the outcome as Unmatched for every dispatch. Phase 2 gives Rejected for Create.
findings.repair: collection-types.md § log of T by P now says dispatch goes on to the next candidate row, and points to spec § 3A.4 phase 2 for what is returned when none matches.

findings.title: §3A.2 item 5 defines Unmatched only for transition rows
findings.reason: Phase 2 returns Unmatched for a stateless precept's on <Event> rows, which are not transition rows. Item 5 had not been widened the way item 6 was.
findings.repair: Spec 3A.2 item 5 now defines Unmatched as Fire having candidate rows (transition rows from the current state, or on a stateless precept the event's on <Event> rows) with every guard false. It notes that the same case at construction is Rejected.

findings.title: The draft says mincount is known at the start of every Fire, which is unsound for a collection the starting state omits and contradicts 3A.4
findings.reason: 3A.4 'What is known', first entry, says a rule that mentions a field the starting state omits is not known of the starting configuration. A modifier is a rule (§2.4). But spec §3.8 'Where mincount discharges an accessor', collection-types.md:786 and proof-engine.md:2093 each said the modifier is known at the start of Fire, Update and Restore with no exception for an omitted collection. Strategy 10 in proof-engine.md, which seeds the count interval from the band, had the same gap, and also for Create and for an optional collection not proved set.
findings.repair: Spec §3.8: the sentence now excepts a collection the starting state omits (what is known of it is its reset value) and an optional collection not proved set, and points to 3A.4. collection-types.md:786 and proof-engine.md:2093 now carry the omitted-collection exception and say the §3.8 note is the full statement. proof-engine.md Strategy 10: a draft-marked paragraph after the delta table says the band seed is not available during Create, for an omitted collection, or for an optional collection not proved set, and points to the 3A.4 entries that say what is known instead.

findings.title: The Restore rule makes a Fire's outcome depend on whether the entity was persisted, under one answer to Known exceptions item 12
findings.reason: The attempt is correct. If a construction row may write a field the initial state omits, the storage holds a value the configuration does not include. Restore slot injection puts the reset value there, so two entities with the same configuration can commit different values from the same Fire, against §0.1 principle 3 (determinism). Item 12's third point, which leaves that write undecided, did not record that the answer reaches Restore and determinism. This is incompleteness in Known exceptions. It does not need a new decision, because the point is already recorded as not stated.
findings.repair: Item 12, third point: added that under the answer allowing such a write, either phase 0's Restore rule or what a configuration includes must change too, against determinism otherwise; under the answer refusing it, neither changes. Nothing assumes an answer.

findings.title: The conditional-expression remedy for the cap can turn an accepted handler into a refused one when the target is optional
findings.reason: Spec §3.6 (String interpolation) says an optional field read 'enrolls a presence obligation exactly as it would in any value position'. The rewrite `set X = if C then 1 else X` adds a read of X that the original lacks, and the two conditions the section listed did not exclude this case. So the explanation could name a remedy that fails.
findings.repair: The cap paragraph now gives three conditions. The third requires every read the remedy adds to be permitted and provably safe where it lands. The paragraph gives the optional Note example and says the conditional rewrite is named only where each set target may be read safely at that position.

findings.title: 'What a patch value may be' does not say what a set or lookup patch that repeats an element or key does
findings.reason: The paragraph refused a repeated key only for log of T by P. For set and lookup it left three possible outcomes for the same patch (Updated, InvalidFields, ConstraintsFailed). Canon does not cover how the JSON lane encodes a set, so the paragraph was incomplete. The consistent rule is the one already stated for log of T by P, applied to the other kinds whose elements or keys are unique.
findings.repair: Added to the first bullet: a value that repeats a set element (under the inner type's comparer) or a lookup key is not a value of the type and fails the type check (InvalidFields, §3A.2 item 9). It is not collapsed. Kinds that keep repeats are unaffected. The four-part reasons are given: reasoning; alternatives rejected (collapse, take as given); precedent (JSON Schema uniqueItems, a database unique key); tradeoff accepted.

findings.title: A write whose right-hand side mentions its own destination carries a false fact forward (set and capture)
findings.reason: Read literally, :2359 carries every fact known of Expr (or of .peek) to the target. That includes facts that read the target's old value, so `Q.peek < D` before `dequeue Q into D` would make `D < D` known. That fact is unsatisfiable, every obligation then discharges, and the definition would be accepted and divide by zero. The informal 'shifted by one' bullet does not restrict the general rule.
findings.repair: In 'A write that replaces a whole value', one stated limit now applies to every carried fact. A fact that also reads a field the action writes (the target, or for a capture the collection or the other target) speaks of that field's old value. It is carried only after the old value is eliminated through the write's own relation, as in `set X = X + 1` shifting a range. Otherwise it is dropped. Examples cover dequeue into D, `set Cap = E.X` and `X == X + 1`. The four-part reasons cite Floyd's forward assignment rule, and the tradeoff respects §0.6's single-fact bound.

findings.title: The section's `from any` dispatch rule contradicts graph-analyzer and builder canon, and the evaluator lookup does not reach `any` rows
findings.reason: The spec's rule follows from canon applied consistently. §2.2 says `any` is 'the state wildcard', and §3A.1 says rows are evaluated 'in declaration order — the first matching guard wins'. graph-analyzer.md §13 also treats a wildcard row and an explicit row that both match as both taken. But graph-analyzer.md §6.1 step 1 gave fallback edge semantics. The precept-builder.md dispatch key comment stored `any` rows under a null key that the evaluator's (state, event) lookup never reads. The spec paragraph also stated the rule without the four-part reasons.
findings.repair: graph-analyzer.md §6.1: an `any` row now produces an edge for every declared state, with a draft-marked paragraph pointing to the spec. precept-builder.md § TransitionDispatchIndex: a draft-marked paragraph says `any` and comma-list rows are placed in each state's list in declaration order, and the key comment now says a null state means a stateless precept only. evaluator.md Fire and InspectFire lookups: a comment says the list already holds the state's own rows, comma-list rows and `any` rows in declaration order. Spec 3A.4 Handlers: added the four-part reasons for the `any` dispatch rule.

findings.title: Two-field quantifier binding for `log of T by P` is decided without a design record
findings.reason: Canon already answers this. collection-types.md says 'two-type-parameter collections expose a two-field binding in quantifier scope', and its Resolved Design Questions item 3 says the binding 'generalizes to all two-type-parameter collections'. The spec's own grammar (§2, `log of CollectionInnerType by CollectionInnerType`) makes log of T by P a two-type-parameter kind. §3.5 gives queue of T by P only as an example. The collection-types Grammar Fit sketch is dated 2026-04-29, before log of T by P was added on 2026-05-01, so it is stale, not a contrary decision. Open Questions (New) item 1 asks whether the binding shape is implicit or explicit, not whether log of T by P has one.
findings.repair: Wording only: the spec's parenthetical now cites both general statements in collection-types.md and the spec grammar, and explains the Grammar Fit sketch omission, rather than arguing from §3.5's silence.

questions.question: Before Create enters the initial state, it evaluates the construction row's guard and actions, a construction reject row's reason, the initial event's argument constraints, and its on-InitialEvent ensures. May any of these read a field the initial state omits? And, as already listed, may the construction row write one?
questions.why_not_answered: Canon disagrees with itself. §3A.5 step 1 builds the hollow version with 'omitted fields structurally absent'. §2.2 D130 refuses reading an omitted field only in the state-anchored contexts it lists, and a construction row is not one of them (§3A.5: 'not yet in any state'). runtime-api.md § Hollow context calls a read of a defaulted field in a construction guard valid, with no exception for an omitted one. The owner's words do not address it.

check.answer_if_any:
No to both. None of the expressions Create evaluates before entering the initial state may read a field the initial state omits. The construction row may not write one either. Canon settles both points once its statements are applied the same way they are applied everywhere else.

1. Writes are refused, as D131 refuses them, and for the same reason. Construction commits a configuration in the initial state: "Create on a stateful precept enters the initial state" (spec:2229, settled 2026-11-25 and committed). The general rule for configurations is that a field the state omits is one where "no write may target it there" (spec:2051). Every other operation that commits a configuration already refuses such a write: D131 for a transition row's target state; the phase 5 text for a no-transition row, which reads D131's "target state" as "the state the row commits in" (spec:2198); and Update's access-mode failure for a patch (spec:1985). Construction would be the only exception.

   The rest of canon holds together only if the write is refused:
   - spec:2199 says Create skips the omit reset "because phase 0 already gave every field the initial state omits its reset value". That is true only if nothing writes the field in between.
   - spec:2344 rests "no writer can change it while the state omits it" on exactly this refusal.
   - spec:2430 itself shows that allowing the write breaks principle 3 (determinism). An entity that was persisted and restored would get the reset value from restore slot injection, while one that was not would keep the row's write. "Under the answer that such a write is refused, neither does [have to change]."

   A consequence follows from D132, which canon calls "the structural dual of InitialEventMissingAssignments". D132 requires an assignment only for a field the target state does not omit. So InitialEventMissingAssignments does not apply to a required field that the initial state omits. That field has no value there, as in any state that omits it, and D132 requires the assignment when a later transition brings it back. This is application, not a new rule.

2. Reads are refused. The hollow version every one of these expressions is evaluated against is built with "initial state set, omitted fields structurally absent" (spec:2515). §3.5 states the general rule, not limited to D130's list of contexts: "reading a structurally absent field is a compile error" (spec:1408, committed 2026-05-12). The 2026-11-25 settlement relies on the same premise: "the fields the initial state omits are absent from what construction builds (§3A.5)" (spec:2229).

   The two texts that seem to point the other way do not:
   - "At construction time, the entity is not yet in any state" (spec:2539) is the reason for the syntax: no `from` prefix. It is not a statement about which fields exist. The settled phase order and step 1 ("initial state set") answer that.
   - runtime-api.md:190-193 makes "Defaulted fields: Valid" on the ground that they "are pre-populated on the hollow version". An omitted field is structurally absent from that version, so the passage says nothing about it either way.

   D130's own reasoning (spec:1128) rejects letting one context read the reset value, because it "decides for this one context what a read of an omitted field means". Allowing it in a construction guard would be exactly that.

What stays open is open for separate reasons, and these are not new owner questions:
- For the initial event's argument constraints and its `on <InitialEvent> ensure` declarations, the answer is conditional. If those may read fields at all, they may not read an omitted one. Whether they may read fields at all is its own open item in spec:2427 ff. (want:143).
- Whether a rule must hold of an omitted field's default in the base case is the first bullet of spec item 12. It concerns rules, not executed reads, and this question does not ask it.

The "not stated" text in Known exceptions item 12 (spec:2430) and the matching exception at spec:2344 should be replaced by this answer, not sent to the owner.

questions.question: Restore receives persisted data that gives a value for a field the persisted state omits. Should it refuse that data as invalid input, or accept it and not write the value?
questions.why_not_answered: runtime-api.md § Restoration lists the only ways Restore can fail: undefined state, unknown fields, type mismatch. A field the state omits is still a declared field, so none of these covers it. No canon text or owner statement says whether such data is invalid or is to be ignored. Either way the field's storage holds its reset value.

check.answer_if_any:
Canon answers both halves. Restore accepts the data, and it does not write the value. Restore must not refuse this data.

1. Accept, do not refuse. Canon lists the ways Restore can fail and closes the list: "the only ways restore can fail are structural: an undefined state name, unknown fields, a type mismatch. `RestoreOutcome` carries those and nothing else" (runtime-api.md:281; spec §3A.2, precept-language-spec.md:2011). A field the persisted state omits is still a declared field, so it is not an "unknown field". Phase 0 defines that check as "every field named is declared" (spec:2147).

Canon also says outright that the current state's per-state field declarations are not checked on restore: "`Restore` accepts all stored fields regardless of the current state's access declarations" (runtime-api.md:283). `omit` is one of those declarations:
- §2.2 says `AccessMode` and `OmitDeclaration` together "govern per-state field access" (spec:1073).
- Composition rule 3 puts `modify|omit` in the same state-level override layer (spec:1111).
- `Update` reports a patch to an omitted field as an "Access mode failure" (spec:1985).

So Restore bypasses `omit` just as it bypasses `readonly` (compiler-and-runtime-design.md:843; evaluator.md:2039). Refusing the data would also mean checking persisted data against the current definition. The owner's words rule that out: restored data is "trusted and unchecked, because it was governed when it was written" (what-i-want-2026-07-16.md:141).

2. Do not write the value. Restore returns the configuration that an earlier operation committed:
- philosophy.md:24: restore "returns a configuration that was already committed".
- spec:2058: "it returns the state and stored field values that an earlier operation committed".

A committed configuration holds no value for a field its state omits, and canon fixes what the storage holds instead: "A field the current state omits ... has no value in this configuration ... What the runtime keeps in the field's storage while the field is omitted is its reset value" (spec:2051, *Configurations* item 2; this text is also in HEAD).

If Restore wrote the persisted value into that storage, a later transition that brings the field back would find that value there. An entity that was never persisted would find the reset value. The two entities hold the same configuration but would commit different results, which breaks §0.1 principle 3 (determinism). The spec makes exactly this argument at Known exceptions item 12 (spec:2430): storage holding something other than the reset value, while restore puts the reset value there, "would then commit a different value from an entity that was persisted and restored than from one that was not, though both hold the same configuration".

So the value is accepted, ignored, and the storage gets the reset value. For a required field without a default, the storage gets no value, and D132 makes the transition that brings the field back assign it. This is the reading the working-tree draft already writes at spec:2147 (phase 0), spec:2267 (the restore slot injection row) and evaluator.md:859.

Caveat for the reviewer: committed HEAD does not agree with itself here. The HEAD writer table says restore slot injection writes "every stored field named in the persisted data" (HEAD precept-language-spec.md:2198). HEAD's *Configurations* item 2 (HEAD:2021) says an omitted field's storage holds its reset value. The draft settles this the way *Configurations* item 2, principle 3 and runtime-api.md:283 require. That is canon applied consistently, not a new decision. The question does not depend on any of the three outstanding owner decisions.

questions.question: May a computed field's `<-` expression call now()? And if a rule or ensure reads such a computed field, does that fall under the outstanding decision on whether rules and ensures may mention now()?
questions.why_not_answered: Canon places no restriction on now() in a computed expression (§3.7, §3.5), and temporal-type-system.md only says 'Guards and actions may read now()'. The want document's open question asks whether time 'belongs only in guards', which may be meant to cover computed fields too. The section is now written to be true either way, and it treats a rule reading such a field as part of decision (b), but the owner has not said whether he sees it that way.

check.answer_if_any:
This is not a new owner question. Both halves are answered. The second half sits inside outstanding decision (b), and canon and the owner's own words already put it there.

1. Can a computed field's `<-` expression call now()? Yes. Committed canon allows it and refuses it nowhere.
- §3.5 gives a computed expression every field name except those that would form a cycle.
- §3.7 lists now() with no position restriction.
- None of the computed-field validation checks in §3.x is about now(); the list is self-reference, transitive cycle, type mismatch, computed-with-default and computed-as-write-target.
- temporal-type-system.md says now() is evaluated with one reading per operation ("same inputs, same outputs within a single fire"). It names guards and actions as readers. That sentence permits; it does not exclude.
- A computed field reading now() asserts nothing. It is evaluated at operation time with that operation's clock reading, the same as an action that reads now(). So the want document's worry does not apply to it on its own terms. That worry is about a claim that "can become false with no event in flight", and only a rule or ensure makes a claim.
- So the field is allowed. Its `<-` fault obligations are discharged at each read position, like any other computed expression.

2. Does a rule or ensure that reads such a field fall under decision (b)? Yes. This follows from canon applied consistently, not from a new ruling.
- Committed canon says a read through a computed field is a read of what it derives from. Spec at HEAD:2180 says "a computed field has no value of its own (*Configurations*), so reading it is reading what it derives from". HEAD:2252 says "A field is read through a computed field as well as directly". D143 says "directly or through a computed-field dependency".
- So a rule that reads `Overdue <- now() > DueDate` mentions the clock through that field, exactly as it would mention `A` through `Gap <- A - B`.
- The owner's open question is defined by what goes wrong, not by spelling. In his words, a time-referencing rule "can become false with no event in flight — nothing writes `today`, there is no ingress point for it, and the inductive model has no step where pure passage of time fits". A rule over a now()-computed field has exactly that property. It is a "rule that references the current moment" in his sense.
- A constraint modifier on such a computed field (for example `max '30 days'` on `Age <- now() - OpenedAt`) is also covered. Modifiers are rule shorthand (§2.4), so it is the same case.

3. What stays open is decision (b) itself. If the owner rules strictly ("time belongs only in guards"), then how far that ruling reaches into computed fields is part of applying (b). It is not a separate question. Until he rules, write nothing that depends on the answer.
- The working-tree text at precept-language-spec.md:2052 and :2689 already takes this position, and its reasoning matches committed canon. It is uncommitted agent text, though, not authority. The authority is the HEAD passages and the want-document line quoted below.

Note: the deleted v1 design docs (commit c987ae32^: PreceptLanguageDesign, ProofEngineDesign, TypeCheckerDesign, EngineDesign, RuntimeApiDesign) say nothing about now(), the clock or "today". the-walk.md and history-rulings.md add nothing beyond the want line and the 2026-08-27 reaffirmation.

questions.question: Must a constraint modifier (a value bound, an inner-type element bound, mincount or maxcount, or a relational modifier like max B) hold after every write that changes a field it constrains, or only of the configuration a handler commits? For example, should 'add Tags E.A -> add Tags E.B' into an optional set with mincount 2 be accepted, since it commits two elements but the first add leaves one?
questions.why_not_answered: Canon gives both answers. §3.5 says a constraint modifier constrains 'the complete configuration rather than any one point in a mutation sequence', and §0.7 states the induction per handler. Against that, §0.6 item 6, §2.3, collection-types.md § Element value modifiers and § Constraints each attach the obligation to every write or every count-changing mutation. The want document (line 20, 'obligations attach to every write site') reads either way. The answer changes which definitions are accepted. It is recorded in spec 3A.4 Known exceptions item 12, and every 'known' fact in 3A.4 is written to be sound under either answer.

check.answer_if_any:
The owner has answered this directly. A constraint modifier holds of the configuration a handler commits, not after every write. The one exception is when the modifier is what keeps an expression from faulting: then it must hold at the point that expression is evaluated.

Why this follows:
1. A constraint modifier desugars to a rule. Spec §2.4 (precept-language-spec.md:1182) says this for all the cardinality and value modifiers, mincount and maxcount included. §2.3 (line 1170) says the same of inner-type element modifiers: each "desugars to a per-element rule". §0.7 says it again for bounds. The v1 design said the same: field constraints "desugar at parse time — field constraints become `rule` nodes ... No new runtime behavior". Every v1 constraint was evaluated once, against the "proposed world (post-mutation, pre-commit)".
2. The owner ruled on when a rule must hold. This is walk item 9, re-asked on 2026-07-26 with a worked handler that breaks a rule part-way through and restores it by the end. He answered "yes, end state only", and the walk records that this "inverts the printed answer for constraints". He then ruled on the fault half with a fault caveat attached, and gave a restatement that is "the one to build against".
3. Read this way, §3.5 ("constrains the complete configuration rather than any one point in a mutation sequence") and §0.7 ("the inductive step is that every handler preserves every rule") agree with the ruling. The other passages say what is owed, not when it is owed:
   - §0.6 item 6, "assignment ... provably outside the target field's constraint range"
   - §2.3, "an element write-site must prove its source within the bound"
   - collection-types § Element value modifiers and § Constraints, "every count-changing mutation ... must prove the count stays in band"
   - want:20, "obligations attach to every write site"
   Each says which writes carry an obligation, the symmetric write site. None says the obligation is judged at that write rather than at commit. Where they are worded per write, that is drift from the ruling, to be corrected toward it. It is not a second answer. history-rulings.md row 40 already records the end-state rule as "not in canon" (searched "end of the handler", "intermediate", "point of evaluation"). So canon has never written the ruling down, which explains the per-write wording.

What follows for the examples:
- `add Tags E.A -> add Tags E.B` into an optional `set` with `mincount 2`, under a guard `E.A != E.B`, commits two elements and is accepted.
- `set A = 20 -> set B = 30` from `B = 10` with `A max B` is accepted.

The fault caveat: if a modifier is what makes an expression fault-free, for example `Months positive` making a division safe, it must hold where that expression is evaluated. The walk calls this a reading of his sentence, not his words, and says to "confirm it rather than assume it". That caveat changes neither example above, because no fault in them depends on mincount or max B.

Spec 3A.4 Known exceptions item 12 (spec:2438) should be closed as answered by walk item 9, not left as an owner question. The per-write wording in §0.6 item 6, §2.3 and collection-types § Element value modifiers and § Constraints should be reconciled to "holds of the committed configuration". The rule-relied-on-for-a-fault caveat should be stated alongside it.

questions.question: Once a transition row has assigned a field that its source state omits (for example the assignment D132 requires), may a later action in the same row read that field? For example, 'set Notes = Submit.N -> set Summary = Notes' from a state that omits Notes.
questions.why_not_answered: §2.2 D130 refuses any read in an action's right-hand side of a field omitted in the anchoring state, with no exception for one the row has written. §2.2 D143 refuses only 'the first assignment that materializes that field', 'directly or through a computed-field dependency', which implies later reads are allowed and would make D143's wording redundant under D130's reading. Canon disagrees with itself and the owner has not ruled. It is recorded in spec 3A.4 Known exceptions item 12 and in phase 5.

check.answer_if_any:
Yes. A later action in the same row may read a field the source state omits once an earlier action in that row has assigned it. In 'set Notes = Submit.N -> set Summary = Notes' from a state that omits Notes, the read of Notes in the second action is allowed. A read of that field before its first assignment stays refused: by D130 in any earlier action, and by D143 inside the first assignment itself, directly or through a computed field.

Why canon already answers this, with nothing stretched:

1. Canon handles the same shape at construction, and that rule is ordered by assignment. At construction a required field with no default has no value until an action gives it one, which is exactly the situation of a field brought back from omit. Canon refuses a read only before the first assignment. PRE0142 refuses the read inside the field's own first assignment, and PRE0144 refuses a read of another field "before that other field's first assignment in the same action chain establishes a value". So a read after that assignment is allowed. D132 calls itself "the structural dual of InitialEventMissingAssignments (D94) applied to state-crossing transitions", and D143 is the transition copy of PRE0142, added in the same commit as PRE0144 (00e68f19). Refusing a read after assignment only for transitions would treat this case differently from construction for no stated reason.

2. Sequencing is a general rule. §0.4 property 3 says "Each assignment in a row sees the state left by all preceding assignments", and §0.6 item 7 says "each subsequent action sees the proof state left by all preceding actions". The owner's fault ruling applies this ordering: a check happens "at the point of evaluation, against the values in force there", and his own Months example (set to 0, then to 12, then divide: compiles) turns on reading a value an earlier action wrote. The v1 language design said the same: "read-your-writes".

3. D130 refuses a read because there is no value to read, not because of the declaration. Its own reasoning: "for a required field without a default there is no value to read at all (§0.1 principle 10)". §3.5 describes the refused read as "reading a structurally absent field". After the row has assigned the field, the working copy holds a value, so that reason does not apply. Reading D130 as refusing every read in the row, with no exception for a field the row wrote, would make D143's limit to "the first assignment" and its word "directly" mean nothing. The reading that keeps both rules meaningful is: D130 covers reads before the assignment, D143 covers the assignment itself, and reads after it are allowed.

4. The draft phase 5 text already says a row's actions read the fields of the source state "as changed by the exit actions and by the row's own earlier actions". Line 2404 already lets the row's actions read a field the target state omits "as ... the row's earlier actions left it". The case asked about is the same rule applied to a field the source state omits.

What still needs doing is editing, not an owner decision: D130's action-RHS clause should carry the exception, a read of a field after an earlier action in the same row has assigned it. Then spec §3A.4 Known exceptions item 12's last entry, its echo in the Open Questions list, and the matching sentence in phase 5 can be removed. This answer does not cover what a computed field that derives from such a field returns elsewhere in the row. That is a separate item-12 entry: a computed expression that mentions a field, in a state that omits it. This answer does not settle it.
